newsitem.title: KENYA: Zaire's Gecamines sanguine on rebel advance.
newsitem.headline: Zaire's Gecamines sanguine on rebel advance.

text.p: An official of Zaire's state-run mineral mining company Gecamines on Thursday said he saw no immediate danger from a rebel advance and hoped a deal would soon be signed with South Africa's Iscor.

"Everything is very calm here and the fighting is very far away, obviously things may change, but it is much too early to say we will be affected," Technical Director Yumba Monga told Reuters by telephone from Zaire's copper and cobalt mining centre of Lubumbashi.
Rebels fighting to topple Zaire's President Mobutu Sese Seko have advanced into the southeastern Shaba region, as far as the port of Kalemie, about 800 km (500 miles), northeast of Lubumbashi.
On Wednesday, rebel leader Laurent Kabila gave President Mobutu Sese Seko until February 21 to surrender power or face a major rebel attack.

But despite the potential threat Yumba said he hoped a deal would soon be signed with South Africa's Iscor for the rehabilitation of the Kamoto mine, which collapsed in 1990 dealing a severe blow to production.
"There has not yet been any negative reaction that I have seen from potential foreign investors who continue to show great interest in us," he said.

Unable to finance itself for any but the smallest operations and with an economically liberal government in Kinshasa, Gecamines has increasingly begun looking at deals with foreign companies as a way to survive.
Foreign companies have expressed more than a tentative interest in some of the world's largest unexploited mineral resources.
"These are long term plans and commitments, and whoever is in power there is going to be interest in developing the resources," said an executive from one company to express an interest.
"Short term security problems are not going to stop interest."
Zaire produces about 5,000 tonnes of cobalt annually, world supply is about 28,000 tonnes, of which 1,000 tonnes is of high grade quality.
A lack of investment in new and existing mining facilities and the belts' infrastructure, as well as years of political and ethnic turmoil, have seen copper production dive dramatically.
London metal analysts estimate that production of contained metal has fallen from 500,000 tonnes in the early 1980s to 210,000 tonnes in 1987 and 33,000 tonnes in 1995.
